trace: Micron is the hardest kind of name to model because everything hinges on where we sit in the memory cycle, and the cycle rarely announces itself. Stock is around $135, above the 50-day EMA at $125 and well above the 200-day SMA at $98, so the trend is intact. RSI at 62 is constructive without being stretched, and OBV confirming price tells me the move is being accumulated rather than short-covered. The MACD histogram shrinking is the one caution flag; it says momentum is cooling even as price holds. Fundamentally MU is still loss-making, so forward P/E is useless and I have to lean on Price/Sales at 4.5x and an EV/Sales framework. If FY2025 revenue lands near $30B and a mid-cycle 4.0x multiple applies, that gets me to roughly $160 as a base case, and I want to weight that at 60 percent because gross margin expansion from 15 to 35 percent over four quarters is a plausible but not heroic path. The bull case is real but narrower: HBM3E and HBM4 demand pulling standard DRAM up with it, a peak-cycle 5.5x on $35B revenue gets $210, and I'd give it 25 percent. Bear case at 15 percent is a false dawn where restocking is mistaken for demand. My honest weakness is timing, my model could be off one or two quarters, and I need to guard against anchoring to the AI narrative when PC and smartphone are still most of the revenue. I'll accumulate here, add on weakness toward $125, and treat a weekly close below $115 as the thesis breaking, with a hard stop under $98.

Block is really two businesses stapled together and the scenario work has to respect that. Square depends on small-business gross payment volume, which is a direct macro read, while Cash App depends on monetization per active user plus a bitcoin overlay that adds noise nobody can forecast. That is why I lean on a DCF flexed across growth and margin assumptions plus a 20,000-iteration Monte Carlo on gross profit growth, BTC price, and transaction volumes rather than pretending a single point estimate is credible. Base case at 60 percent has GPV up 10 to 12 percent, Cash App gross profit up around 20 percent, BTC range-bound $55,000 to $75,000, and adjusted operating margin up 100 to 150 basis points. At 25x forward EV/gross profit, slightly under the historical average to reflect maturation, I get $80. Bull at 25 percent needs a soft landing plus a genuine new Cash App product. Bear at 15 percent is two negative GDP quarters, unemployment above 5 percent, Borrow loan losses running past provisions, BTC under $40,000 forcing a writedown, and CFPB rules biting Afterpay; a compressed 15x gets $45. Probability-weighting lands at $82.50, which is uncomfortably close to where the stock already trades. That is the whole judgment: the math does not pay me to buy here. So Hold, wait for the $60 to $65 zone, and only chase on a weekly close above $90 with volume or two quarters of Cash App gross profit above 25 percent. With beta above 2.0 I would size any position at half normal and set the stop at $57.50 just under the $58 support.

For NVIDIA at roughly $950 the central question is not whether AI demand is real but how long the current shape of it persists, so I want a Monte Carlo over data center growth, competition, and macro rather than a single-path model. Base case, 60 percent, assumes data center revenue compounds 120 to 150 percent year over year for four more quarters on hyperscaler capex, AMD's MI300X takes a respectable but non-threatening 5 to 10 percent, and CUDA keeps switching costs prohibitive. Applying 40x forward earnings, a modest compression from today to reflect growth maturing, gives $1150. The bull at 25 percent needs demand pulled forward from 2026 and 2027, a successful China-compliant part like H20, and real software monetization through AI Enterprise and Omniverse; 50x supports $1450. The bear at 15 percent is where I have to be honest: a full ban on high-end China sales removes roughly 20 percent of data center revenue with no substitute, or the build-out proves one-time and an air pocket appears in mid-2025. My sensitivity work says a 10 percent cut to expected data center growth takes about $90 off fair value, which is a useful calibration. Self-critique matters here. I am probably carrying recency bias, overweighting spectacular recent quarters against a semiconductor industry that has always been cyclical, and the 75 percent gross margins are a function of scarcity, not physics; normalization to 60 to 65 percent alone argues for something near the bear target. I set base conviction at 75 percent and only 60 percent on the bull and bear splits since those hinge on geopolitics. Early warnings: two quarters of rising days of inventory, guidance below 70 percent gross margin, or H100 lead times collapsing from 40 weeks toward 12.

Exxon is a macro-levered equity with a company-specific quality overlay, so I want the scenarios driven by WTI and crack spreads simulated 10,000 times, valued through a two-stage dividend discount model cross-checked against EV/EBITDA versus the ten-year sector average. Base case, 60 percent, has WTI averaging $75 to $85 with OPEC+ holding discipline, ROE settling at 15 to 18 percent, FCF yield of 8 to 10 percent, low single-digit production growth from Guyana and the Permian, and the $17.5B buyback continuing. Technically the stock keeps oscillating between the 200-day SMA near $108 and resistance near $120, MACD hovering at the zero line, RSI penned between 45 and 65 - a genuinely balanced tape. A 6.5x forward EV/EBITDA gets me $125. The bull case at 25 percent needs WTI sustained above $100 from a supply shock or a China recovery, ROE above 25 percent, EPS growth over 30 percent, and a break of the $124 high, which supports $150. The bear at 15 percent breaks the 200-day and $100, prints a death cross with distribution on OBV, and compresses to 5.0x for $90. Weighting those gives $126.25, comfortably above spot, so Accumulate rather than aggressively buy. I would scale in between $110 and $115, add above $125 on a weekly close, and cut on a weekly close below $105. My honest concern is the terminal-value trap: if energy transition de-rates the whole sector permanently, this base case consolidation is actually a topping pattern, and the thin volume on recent rallies is consistent with that reading. If $105 breaks I check WTI below $70, IMF growth revisions, and Guyana ramp news first.

This NVIDIA framing is anchored on a much lower share price than the pre-split view, so I am working with a stock consolidating roughly $115 to $130 and building targets off consensus FY26 EPS of $3.88. Base case at 60 percent applies 40x to that, giving $155, and rests on data center growing 35 to 40 percent year over year with gaming recovering to 5 to 10 percent after its inventory correction, gross margin above 75 percent, operating margin above 55 percent, and ROE above 80 percent. The technical read supports it: price holding above the 50-day EMA, RSI parked between 50 and 65, MACD histogram positive. My stated vulnerability is competitive, and I want it explicit - this only works if AMD's MI300X plus hyperscaler in-house silicon take under 15 percent of incremental accelerator demand, so I hold confidence at 75 percent and treat two consecutive quarters of sub-30 percent data center growth as invalidation, checking TSMC CoWoS capacity first. Bull at 25 percent needs AI Enterprise software passing 10 percent of data center revenue plus outsized Blackwell gains, which earns 50x and $190. Bear at 15 percent is $100 on custom silicon displacement plus a capex freeze; a funds rate above 5.5 percent cutting IT budgets 10 to 15 percent flows through to a 15 to 20 percent hit to enterprise growth. Weighted, that is $153.25, which supports Accumulate. Practically: start in the $120 to $125 zone, cap at 5 to 7 percent of a growth book given beta above 1.5, exit on a weekly close below the 200-day near $98, and trim half immediately if Commerce announces substantive new China restrictions.

Nine months is a short leash for a cyclical like Micron, so I want to be precise about what the recovery actually delivers inside that window. Base case at 60 percent assumes DRAM and NAND contract prices rising 5 to 10 percent sequentially each quarter, HBM3E shipping to plan, and PCs and phones recovering only in single digits. That supports gross margins back to 30 to 35 percent and a forward P/S near 6.5x; putting 7.0x on FY2025 consensus revenue gives $160, and I hold 75 percent confidence because it matches channel checks and guidance. Technically the setup cooperates: price above the 50-day EMA, RSI in the 60 to 70 band, and a real volume shelf at $120 to $125 that gives me a defensible invalidation level. The bull at 25 percent is where the leverage is, and the transmission math is what makes it credible rather than hand-waving: every 5 percent shift of revenue mix into HBM at 60 percent gross margin versus 30 percent for standard DRAM adds roughly $0.25 to quarterly EPS, which justifies both higher earnings and a higher multiple toward $200. Weighting everything gives $157. My discomfort is that the multiple has already expanded on the HBM narrative, so the stock is priced for execution and a stumble de-rates it hard, and the honest alternative reading is that this is aggressive restocking that ends in an air pocket. That is why I say accumulate on weakness rather than buy here: scale in $130 to $140 near the 50-day EMA, add above $165, and exit on a decisive break of $120. If MU lags while SOX holds up, I check TrendForce contract prices, Samsung and SK Hynix capex, and ASML and Lam backlogs.

Working NVIDIA off forward earnings means my whole answer lives inside two assumptions, the EPS path and the multiple, so I should be explicit about both. The base case at 55 percent has share above 80 percent in data center accelerators, FY2025 revenue up 65 percent then FY2026 up 30 percent, and China handled through compliant chip variants. On projected FY2026 EPS of $35.00 I apply 35x, slightly under where the stock trades, because decelerating growth deserves some compression, and that yields $1,225 over eighteen months with ROE still north of 80 percent. Technically I want the 50-day EMA holding as dynamic support, RSI in the 55 to 70 zone, and the $800 to $850 volume shelf as the floor. Bull at 30 percent takes Blackwell adoption above 50 percent in its first year with networking and software carrying the mix; $42.00 EPS at 40x gives $1,680. Bear at 15 percent is a hyperscaler digestion pause plus AMD or Intel taking 15 to 20 percent share and forcing margins down from 75 percent. I score fundamentals at 85 percent confidence, the competitive read at only 60 percent, and the multiple assumption at 70 percent, which is the weakest link. I have to flag recency bias openly, and note that 55 percent on the base may be too conservative if this is early innings. The two opposite readings both deserve air: NVIDIA as the operating system of AI, where even bull EPS is low, versus a Cisco-2000 setup where any miss cuts the stock in half. The first tell either way is sequential data center gross margin, ahead of revenue.

This is a nine to twelve month NVIDIA call built on the post-split price scale, and my anchor is the Hopper to Blackwell transition executing without a demand gap. Base case at 55 percent keeps share near 80 percent, data center revenue up 90 percent year over year while decelerating toward 30 percent sequentially by mid-2025, gross margins steady at 75 to 77 percent, ROCE above 100 percent, and a forward multiple settling at 35x. On roughly $4.14 forward EPS that is $145. The technical condition I want is price above the 50-day EMA with RSI cooling from above 70 through consolidation rather than sharp breaks, and OBV still rising to confirm institutional accumulation. Bull at 30 percent needs Blackwell demand exceeding supply for eighteen months, a sovereign AI deal above $5 billion, and AMD underwhelming, which pushes margins to 78 to 80 percent. Bear sits at 15 percent, and my stress test - a 20 percent cut to data center growth plus 500 basis points of margin compression, essentially replaying 2018 - lands fair value near $100, which is exactly where I put the bear target, so the framework is internally consistent. What I keep circling back to in self-critique is that this revenue is capex from a handful of buyers, not recurring subscription revenue, so it is structurally less stable than the multiple implies, and recency bias is a live risk. That is why I name demand normalization at 35 percent as the single most likely failure mode: a 30 to 40 percent multiple contraction without an earnings collapse. Watch DIO rising two quarters, order push-outs at Dell or SMCI, AMD data center GPU revenue above $4 billion, and if the 100-day breaks on volume, check Azure and Google capex guidance and TSMC HPC revenue.

A six to nine month window on NVIDIA compresses everything into the next two earnings prints, so I want scenarios that are checkable on that cadence rather than vague multi-year stories. Base case at 60 percent has revenue growth decelerating to 80 to 100 percent year over year from prior levels above 200 percent, gross margins stabilizing at 75 to 76 percent, and the multiple easing to 35 to 40x. Applying 40x to $3.63 forward EPS gives $145. The technical condition is consolidation above the 50-day EMA with RSI cooling from overbought into the 55 to 65 range and OBV rising, which is what a healthy base looks like rather than a blowoff. Bull at 25 percent needs two straight quarters of 20 percent-plus revenue beats, multi-billion sovereign AI deals, and visible CUDA monetization, taking the stock toward $180. Bear compresses the multiple to 25 to 30x on lower revenue and margins; 30x on $3.17 gives $95, with the tell being a decisive loss of the 50-day EMA turning it into resistance and the accumulation-distribution line rolling over. I set fundamental confidence at 85 percent, technical at 75 percent, and probability calibration at only 60 percent, because the AI market's evolution is genuinely unmapped. The honest critique is that I am leaning on sell-side forward EPS in a market where those estimates get revised violently, and that insider selling plus the valuation could mean the bull case is already in the price. Practically: hold a core position, express the bull with calls to cap risk, buy dips toward $115 to $120, and stop near $110 if the 50-day fails for three consecutive closes.

Shopify's whole debate reduces to whether a premium multiple survives normalized e-commerce growth, so I want the scenarios keyed to gross profit rather than revenue, since that is what the market actually pays for here. Base case at 60 percent assumes GMV growing 18 to 22 percent, subscription solutions up around 25 percent on Plus adoption, and operating margin expanding 150 to 200 basis points now that logistics is divested. At 16x forward EV/gross profit that is $72, with the stock chopping between $55 and $75 and the 200-day acting as dynamic support. Bull at 25 percent requires a soft landing plus real traction from Shopify Magic and B2B, evidenced by two quarters of GMV above 25 percent and take rate past 3.1 percent; 20x supports $95 on a volume-confirmed break of $75. Bear at 15 percent is discretionary spending contracting, which compresses the multiple to 12x and gives $48. I'd put overall thesis confidence at 65 percent, valuation confidence only 55 percent because it is so growth-sensitive, and technical confidence at 75 percent since the range is clean. The uncomfortable alternative reading is that the sideways action is distribution, not accumulation, and at roughly 60x forward earnings there is no margin of safety to absorb a miss. I also have to check myself for anchoring to the old highs above $150; the post-ZIRP paradigm is different. Failure signals in order: merchant solutions decelerating faster than subscriptions, take rate compression, and a run of downward estimate revisions. The most likely failure mode is stagflationary, roughly 30 percent likely with about 25 percent price impact, and the Adobe subscription-transition analog fits the volatile consolidation.

The core question I keep testing on Micron is whether AI has genuinely changed the amplitude of the memory cycle or merely delayed it. My base case at 60 percent says softened, not abolished: a cyclical upturn where HBM3E revenue at high margin dampens the boom-bust, revenue accelerating 40 to 50 percent year over year, gross margins moving from low single digits to 25 to 30 percent, and forward P/E compressing to about 15x as earnings actually appear against today's negative GAAP EPS. The chart supports that framing with price basing above the 200-day SMA at $85 and riding the 50-day EMA at $110, MACD above signal, RSI in the 60 to 70 zone. That gets me $145 over nine to twelve months. The bull at 25 percent needs Samsung and SK Hynix yield problems handing Micron pricing power while HBM passes 25 percent of the mix at 50 percent-plus margins; my sensitivity says each 500 basis points of corporate gross margin above base adds roughly $15 per share, and 8x peak-cycle EV/Sales supports $190. The bear at 15 percent is symmetric and simple: a 10 percent decline in blended ASPs pushes margins back toward zero and takes the stock to $95 at the 200-day. I want to be blunt in critique that treating AI demand as secular rather than a longer-wavelength cycle is my biggest exposure, that recency bias may be inflating HBM relative to the far larger traditional markets, and that 15 percent on the bear may understate recession risk. Go long near the 50-day around $110, use calls to define risk, and stop out below $85 on volume.

Nine months out, Micron trades near $130 and I need scenario spacing that respects how violently this name moves. I set the base at 55 percent rather than the usual 60 because the cycle genuinely could break either way: sequential price improvement in DRAM and NAND, HBM3E ramping to consensus, revenue up 45 percent, gross margins reaching 35 to 40 percent, ROE around 18 percent, and forward P/E expanding to roughly 15x against a historical average near 10x, which I can defend only by pointing to the structural AI component. That gives $140, with the stock likely oscillating $120 to $145 on the 50-day EMA, RSI between 50 and 70. Bull at 30 percent is unusually fat for me, justified by the possibility that HBM prices rise more than 20 percent quarterly and enterprise SSDs more than 10 percent while competitors stumble on yields, pushing gross margins past 50 percent and the stock to $165. Bear at 15 percent gives $105 on demand disappointment and inventory glut. Weighted, that is $141.50, so Buy. The backtest is the part I trust most and least at once: across twelve prior memory cycles, once gross margins cross 20 percent off the trough the stock rose over the following two quarters 75 percent of the time, but the median drawdown along the way was still 18 percent, which tells me to size at about 4 percent given the beta and to expect pain even when right. I would also grant 25 percent odds that rising capex signals future oversupply rather than confidence. Add above $145, worry below $118, hard stop $104.

Palantir over six months is really a bet on how fast AIP pilots convert into signed enterprise contracts, and I do not have clean visibility into that, so I should hold overall confidence around 65 percent - technicals at 70 percent, fundamentals at 60 percent given the stretched valuation, catalysts at 65 percent. Base case at 60 percent has commercial revenue compounding 35 to 40 percent while government holds at 15 to 20 percent, GAAP profitability extending to a fifth and sixth consecutive quarter, and operating margins widening 50 to 100 basis points a quarter. That combination makes S&P 500 inclusion a live catalyst in the back half of the window, which is worth something mechanically as well as narratively. On a 20x forward EV/Sales multiple, modestly above the historical average because of the AI premium, I get $28, with the stock consolidating $20 to $27 above a 200-day SMA near $18.50, weekly MACD above signal and daily RSI between 50 and 65. Bull at 25 percent needs a genuine demonstrated ROI moment and Fortune 100 contracts, which at 28x EV/Sales gives $40 in an NVIDIA-style re-rating. My weaknesses are real: I may be anchoring price targets to historical multiples that no longer apply if this is a durable paradigm, I lean too much on AIP while Gotham and Foundry still carry the base, and the platform's actual scalability is opaque to outsiders. The stock-based compensation could be read either as dilution the market will eventually punish or as the cost of AI talent that nobody cares about while growth holds. Early bear tells: lengthening sales cycles, unusual 10b5-1 selling by Karp or Thiel, trouble at a top-20 customer.

Running the full framework on NVIDIA, the honest overall confidence is about 70 percent, high on fundamentals, medium on technicals given how violently this trades, low on macro. Base case at 60 percent uses 40x forward earnings on FY2026 consensus EPS of $3.62, which is in line with the three-year average premium rather than the peak multiple, deliberately, to keep recency bias in check. That yields $145, with support at the 50-day EMA at $118, RSI between 55 and 65, and OBV still rising. The one wrinkle is a positive but contracting MACD histogram, which reads as consolidation rather than reversal. Fundamentals underneath are 85 percent revenue growth, ROE at 70 percent, ROCE at 55 percent, and gross margins near 75 percent, with data center up 90 percent and Blackwell shipping without incident. Bull at 25 percent goes to 48x for $175, with the sensitivity I trust: each 1 percent move in global AI infrastructure spending forecasts flows through to roughly 1.8 percent on data center revenue. The bear pivots on rates, where 200 basis points of tightening cuts IT budgets 5 to 7 percent and forward orders 10 to 15 percent, with a technical trigger of three closes below the 100-day at $105. What nags at me is the alternative reading that this consolidation is distribution, and ADX at 28 does hint at weakening trend strength. So accumulate on weakness rather than chase: buy $118 to $122, target $145, stop $104, and if that stop breaks, check hyperscaler order cuts and whether the VIX is above 25.

Exxon over twelve months comes down to how much of the outcome the company actually controls, which is why I split confidence: 85 percent on fundamentals because the balance sheet and capital allocation framework are genuinely legible, only 60 percent on commodity prices, 70 percent on the scenario weights. The base case at 60 percent has Brent between $75 and $95, capex held to $23 to $25 billion, the $17.5 billion buyback continuing, ROCE above 15 percent, FCF yield of 8 to 9 percent, and a forward P/E near 11.5x that still looks cheap against the index. The stock keeps working between the 200-day SMA around $108 and resistance near $120 with a modest positive MACD histogram and OBV showing steady accumulation. A 6.5x EV/EBITDA multiple on base-case EBITDA gets me $130. Bull at 25 percent requires Brent sustained above $100, Guyana beating guidance by 5 percent, and a real Low Carbon Solutions deal, which supports 7.5x and $155. Bear at 15 percent is a hard landing in China and Europe. I would accumulate $110 to $115, add above $125, review on a weekly close under $108, and cut size below $100. Two things keep me honest. First, the base case quietly assumes OPEC+ stays cohesive, which is a geopolitical bet, not a financial one. Second, there is maybe a 30 percent case that the enormous buyback signals an absence of attractive transition investments rather than confidence. If the $130 target fails, I check the 3:2:1 crack spread for a sustained drop under $20, whether cash flow is falling faster than net income, and any unexplained slowdown in buyback pace.

KeyCorp is a two-variable problem over three to six months: where net interest margin bottoms and how much credit stress the commercial real estate book actually contains. I am comfortable putting 80 percent confidence on the NIM path but only 60 percent on credit, because office CRE health is genuinely opaque across the whole industry, which pulls overall confidence to about 70 percent. My base case at 65 percent has the Fed on hold, NIM compressing another 5 to 8 basis points before stabilizing as deposit cost increases decelerate, net charge-offs rising to 0.45 to 0.55 percent of average loans, and loan growth roughly flat. If the market simply stops pricing crisis, a re-rating to 1.1x price to tangible book - still below the historical average - supports $15.50, and history says regional banks with this profile returned 8 to 12 percent over six months in comparable post-hiking stable-rate periods. The bull at 20 percent is a clean rate-cut signal, and my sensitivity is that each 25 basis points off fed funds adds 4 to 6 basis points of forward NIM, worth roughly $0.75 per share, taking the target to $19.00. The bear at 15 percent takes NCOs to 0.80 to 1.00 percent and de-rates to 0.8x tangible book for $10.00, with the specific failure mode being one large CRE default forcing a dilutive capital raise. Weighted that is $15.63, so Buy, entering near the 50-day around $13.75, trimming at $15.50, exiting on a weekly close under the 200-day at $12.50. My real vulnerability is that this whole thing is a Fed call and misreading Fedspeak breaks it.

Block over nine to twelve months forces me to model two engines with different macro sensitivities, so I run the DCF probability-weighted with the segment gross profit assumptions stressed separately and calibrate the odds against options-implied volatility. Overall confidence lands at 65 percent, which is honest given how wide the outcome distribution is. Base case at 55 percent has Cash App gross profit up 20 percent on Cash App Card and Borrow monetization while Square grows a resilient 10 percent as small businesses stabilize, adjusted EBITDA margin widening 150 basis points, the company hitting Rule of 40 for 2026, and P/S normalizing near 3.0x against its three-year median. Technically I want a base above the 200-day around $60, RSI between 50 and 65, and the high-volume node at $65 to $70 as support. Fifteen times forward EV/gross profit gives $95. Bull at 25 percent requires two quarters of Cash App gross profit above 25 percent, a new high-margin product, and a Fed cutting cycle, pushing total gross profit growth past 25 percent and margins up more than 300 basis points. Weighted, I get $94.75 against a stock near $70, which supports Buy with a partial position now and adds above $75. The counterargument I take seriously is that the pivot to profitability means hyper-growth is over and Block becomes a slower, utility-like fintech that never earns the bull multiple, in which case today's price is fair at best. Stop on a weekly close under $58. Canaries: Cash App transacting users stalling, GPV per seller falling, or management conceding pricing pressure.

AMD sits awkwardly between two stories, a solid CPU share-gain business and a speculative AI accelerator option, and the valuation only works if the second one delivers something. Base case at 60 percent assumes MI300X takes 10 to 15 percent of the accelerator market by end of 2025 while AMD defends its number two server CPU position, revenue compounding at an 18 percent CAGR, gross margin up 150 basis points to 52.5 percent on richer data center mix, ROE near 20 percent, and the forward multiple compressing from 45x to a more defensible 35x. On FY2025 EPS of $5.43 that gives $190. Technically the stock is consolidating between its 50-week and 100-week SMAs with RSI in the 45 to 60 band and a clear volume shelf at $145 to $155, which is consistent with a range rather than a trend. Bull at 25 percent needs the moat to crack: 25 percent-plus accelerator share, with my sensitivity showing each 1 point of share worth roughly $2 billion of revenue and $0.75 of EPS, supporting 45x and $285 on a breakout above the $227 high. Bear at 15 percent is a cyclical trough at 25x on reduced EPS of $4.80, so $120. Weighted that is $197.25 against roughly $160, so I initiate long and scale $150 to $165. I hold thesis confidence at 75 percent but valuation model accuracy at only 65 percent, because everything bullish depends on ROCm actually challenging CUDA and on MI300 orders I cannot verify. Stop on a weekly close below the 200-day near $148, then check Intel server wins, channel checks on MI300, and TSMC revisions.

Micron's setup here is technically clean, which is exactly when I should be most careful. Price is above the 20, 50, and 200-day EMAs, MACD is positive above signal, RSI at 68 is strong without being extreme, and the breakout above $130 has turned that level into support. That earns 75 percent technical confidence, but I only give 60 percent to my scenario probabilities because timing memory cycles is where analysts consistently embarrass themselves. Base case at 65 percent has HBM demand plus a traditional server, PC, and phone rebound driving pricing power and margin expansion, with a 2.5x P/B today looking reasonable if peak profitability returns; applying a 3.0x forward P/B in line with prior cyclical peaks gives $165 over six to nine months. Bull at 25 percent requires HBM supply to fall short of AI accelerator demand, and my transmission estimate is that each 10 percent expansion of the HBM TAM lifts total revenue about 4 percent with roughly 1.5x that impact on gross profit given the mix; a 4.0x P/B with ROCE above 25 percent supports $210. Bear sits at only 10 percent, a false dawn. What I want to state plainly is the vulnerability: this assumes a flawless HBM3E ramp, and much of the move so far is multiple expansion rather than delivered earnings, so a small stumble de-rates the stock hard, and the high-volume breakout could equally read as a blow-off top. Watch DDR5 and HBM contract prices flattening two weeks running, days of inventory failing to fall, Samsung or SK Hynix cutting price, and any hyperscaler using the word optimization.

Taking NVIDIA through the full framework at roughly $125, the technical picture and the valuation picture pull in opposite directions and I need to hold both. Price is above the 20 and 50-day EMAs, it broke out of the $120 consolidation, OBV is climbing steeply which tells me institutions are buying, and it is walking the upper Bollinger band. But daily RSI at 72 is overbought and the MACD histogram is shrinking even as price makes highs, so the odds of a pause are elevated and I should watch for outright RSI divergence. Fundamentally there is very little to argue with: 78 percent gross margins, 55 percent net margin, debt to equity of 0.25, revenue growth above 80 percent for the next two quarters, 80 to 90 percent share in accelerators, and a PEG around 1.2 that makes the 45x forward multiple defensible despite looking rich in isolation. The FCF yield of only 2.2 percent is the reminder that a lot is priced in. My bear case runs a 10 percent cut to data center sales plus 500 basis points of margin compression, de-rating to about 30x for $95. So the recommendation writes itself: accumulate rather than chase, take a third of the position here and add toward the 50-day at $115, entry zone $115 to $125, and treat a weekly close under $100 as invalidating the uptrend and pushing bear odds above 30 percent. Confidence: 85 percent on fundamentals, 70 percent on technicals given the overbought reading, 60 percent on valuation, which is where the real risk lives - air pocket risk from crowded positioning.

Snowflake at roughly $155 is a bottoming argument, not a momentum one, and I want the scenarios to reflect that. The base case at 60 percent assumes consumption trends stabilize and product revenue re-accelerates into the low 30s percent year over year as Cortex and Snowpark Container Services start monetizing AI workloads, with non-GAAP operating margin reaching about 8 percent, RPO growth holding near 35 percent, and FCF margin around 25 percent. The chart supports a base above $140, which lines up with the 200-week SMA, bullish MACD divergence on the daily, and RSI lifting out of oversold inside a $140 to $180 consolidation. At 17x EV/forward revenue - a discount to history that respects the more mature growth profile - I get $175, with P/S contracting to about 16x forward. Bull at 25 percent needs product growth above 40 percent for two straight quarters plus a big guidance raise, taking me to $220. I hold fundamental thesis confidence at 70 percent and valuation model confidence at 75 percent, but only 65 percent on the probabilities themselves. My blind spots deserve naming: everything here assumes the market keeps paying a premium multiple, so a broad tech de-rating breaks the targets even if the numbers land; the consumption model is lumpier than RPO implies, especially with sporadic AI training workloads; and 15 percent on the bear may be too generous to Snowflake given how fast Databricks and the lakehouse architecture are moving. Start with a partial position here, build if it reclaims the 50-day near $162, trim at $175, hard stop on a weekly close under $138, and if it stalls in a rising tape check net revenue retention against the 125 percent line first.

Adobe near $525 is the classic incumbent-versus-disruption question and the whole 6 to 9 month debate is whether Firefly is a revenue driver or a cost of staying relevant. Base case at 60 percent has Firefly integrating cleanly across Creative, Experience, and Document Cloud with a modest ARPU uplift, revenue up 11 percent, operating margins holding near 36 percent, FCF yield about 3.5 percent, and ROE above 40 percent. Thirty times forward earnings, just under the five-year average, gives $550, with the stock ranging between 200-day support at $510 and $580 resistance, RSI stuck at 45 to 60 and MACD flat around zero, which is exactly the tape a no-catalyst consolidation produces. Bull at 25 percent requires enterprise AI contracts with demonstrable ROI and Canva and Figma failing to breach the professional base, pushing revenue to 15 to 17 percent growth and the multiple to 36x for $675, confirmed by a volume break above $580. Bear at 15 percent has generative AI commoditizing and good-enough alternatives forcing churn or price cuts, compressing to 24x for $420. My discomfort is real: the contrarian case is that specialized tools like Sora and Midjourney unbundle the creative workflow, which would erode the suite advantage that justifies the premium, and I may be carrying a halo effect from Adobe's execution history. The likeliest failure mode is not lost revenue but margin compression from GPU and inference costs, so I would watch COGS and R&D as a share of revenue, plus Digital Media net new ARR falling under $400 million. Buy here, add near $510, stop $480.

Block near $70 is a genuinely balanced setup and I should resist manufacturing conviction. Confidence splits usefully: 70 percent on fundamentals, 75 percent on technicals since the range behavior is clear, but only 60 percent on scenario probabilities because they hinge on Fed policy and consumer spending. Base case at 60 percent assumes a soft landing with inflation at 2.5 to 3.0 percent and one or two 25 basis point cuts late in the window, Cash App gross profit growing 20 to 25 percent, Square GPV up 8 to 10 percent, and adjusted EBITDA margins improving 150 basis points from cost cuts. The stock keeps working inside $55 to $85 with the 200-day near $68 as support and RSI oscillating 40 to 65. At 25x forward EV/EBITDA, slightly under the historical average, that gives $82. Bull at 25 percent needs 100 basis points-plus of cuts, Cash App Pay adoption pushing Square GPV growth above 15 percent, and Cash App gross profit past 30 percent. What tempers me is the alternative reading that the stagnation reflects US saturation for Cash App rather than macro, and the competitive threat from Zelle in P2P and Toast in restaurant POS could permanently cap Square. So stance is neutral to cautiously optimistic: accumulate $65 to $70 targeting $80, add only on a volume break above $85, exit on a weekly close under $55, size at 2 to 3 percent, and consider long-dated calls to define risk. If $55 breaks, check GPV per seller, the first sequential decline in Cash App actives, and credit loss provisions in the 10-Q.

Shell trades near $76 and I want to test whether the cheapness is real or a value trap on transition risk. I model the outcomes with a 15,000-iteration Monte Carlo across oil, gas, and refining margins off the forward curves, then adjust the weights for geopolitical risk. Base case at 60 percent has Brent between $75 and $90, capital discipline maintained, buybacks running about $3.5 billion a quarter, FCF yield of 10 to 12 percent, ROE at 14 to 15 percent, and a P/E near 9.5x, below the five-year average. Applying 10.5x to projected EPS of $8.00 gives $84, with the 200-day at $72 as the floor, RSI at 45 to 60, and OBV showing steady accumulation inside a long ascending channel. The bull at 25 percent is straightforward leverage: every $10 on Brent adds roughly $1.25 to annual EPS, so a spike to $100 to $120 plus stronger LNG pricing takes EPS above $10.00 and the stock to $105 at the same 10.5x. Bear at 15 percent is a demand hit of 2 to 3 million barrels a day, a 15 percent windfall tax, and forced allocation into 6 to 8 percent IRR renewables against 15 to 20 percent oil projects, dragging ROCE under 10 percent for $65 on 9.0x and $7.20 EPS. Probability-weighted that is $80.50, about 6 percent upside, which is modest but supported by a big shareholder return. Enter near $76, trim at $84, add if Brent holds above $95, hard stop $69 to cap downside near 9 percent.

For a twelve-month NVIDIA view I want the confidence scores to do real work, because they expose where the argument is weak. I am at 90 percent on the fundamental AI dominance thesis, 75 percent on near-term technicals, 60 percent on geopolitical impact, and only 55 percent on valuation - that last number is the honest core of the problem. Base case at 65 percent has data center revenue up 90 percent, gaming recovering modestly, ROIC above 50 percent, FCF conversion above 95 percent of net income, and the forward multiple compressing to about 45x purely because earnings grow into it. On FY2026 EPS of $3.22 that is $145, with appreciation front-loaded into the first half after strong prints and consolidation after. Bull at 25 percent is 55x for $180 on Blackwell demand exceeding supply and a consumer AI upgrade cycle, though I note the weekly RSI reaching 85 to 90 in that path would itself look like a blow-off. Bear gives $95 at 30x on cut estimates, with the primary tail risk being TSMC disruption in Taiwan rather than competition. The alternative interpretation I assign 30 percent odds to is that current demand is a one-time pull-forward as everyone races to build foundation models, making the digestion phase deeper than the market assumes. Because the stock is priced for near-perfection, I would accumulate on weakness rather than buy at the highs, entering near the 50-day around $118, adding above $140 on volume, and abandoning the thesis on a weekly close below the 200-day near $90. Tells: data center gross margin slipping, inventory days spiking, hyperscalers talking about optimizing existing capacity.

The interesting thing about NVIDIA on a twelve-month view is that my confidence in the business and my confidence in the price are nowhere near each other. I would put the AI dominance thesis at 85 percent and momentum at 75 percent, but valuation sustainability at only 40 percent, which drags overall forecast confidence to 65 percent. Base case at 55 percent has share holding above 80 percent, revenue decelerating from hyper-growth to a still-remarkable 60 to 80 percent, EPS up about 75 percent, and the forward multiple compressing from 40x to 35x. On FY2026 EPS near $4.14 that is $145, and I expect that path to include 15 to 20 percent pullbacks to the 50-day EMA rather than a smooth ride. Bull at 30 percent needs a second infrastructure wave plus delays at AMD's MI400 and Intel's Falcon Shores, keeping operating margins above 65 percent and the multiple at 45x for $190. What tempers everything is the backtest: across twenty prior hyper-growth names trading above 30x forward, 60 percent suffered a drawdown greater than 25 percent within eighteen months even when fundamentals stayed intact. That is a statement about multiple risk, not business risk, and it is why I recommend trimming 10 to 15 percent of an existing position rather than adding here, and why new money should wait for the 50-day. My stress test shows a 10 percent cut to data center growth alone takes the base target to about $130. Watch H100 and B200 lead times shortening, Microsoft or Meta capex language, and AMD data center upside surprises.

Micron on a twelve-month horizon needs quantified pricing assumptions or the whole thing is just narrative. Base case at 60 percent has DRAM ASPs rising 15 to 20 percent sequentially for two quarters, HBM3E climbing to 25 percent of total revenue by the fourth quarter of 2024, gross margins reaching 40 to 45 percent by mid-2025, and revenue growth accelerating past 50 percent year over year by early 2025. On 18x forward earnings against FY2025 EPS of $9.00 that gives $162, supported technically by price above upward-sloping 50-day and 200-day EMAs, RSI at 55 to 65, and prior resistance at $120 now acting as support. Bull at 25 percent is a genuine repeat of 2017 to 2018: ASPs up more than 30 percent sequentially, gross margins past 55 percent, and cycle-peak 22x on $11.50 EPS giving $253. Bear at 15 percent falls back to a trough 2.0x price to book for $95, with a 10 percent decline in PC and smartphone units cutting revenue 5 to 7 percent and stalling margin recovery at 25 percent. Weighted, that is $152, which is a favorable skew. What I want to flag against myself is that HBM, however exciting, is still the smaller part of the business, so leaning the thesis on it is a form of recency bias, and there is a real chance this is buy the rumor and the entire 2025 recovery is already priced, so an in-line print alone could trigger a momentum unwind. If $120 breaks, check TrendForce spot data, ASML and Lam capex commentary, and whether days of inventory actually fell.

With Palantir the segment split is what determines how much I can actually claim to know: government at 85 percent confidence because contracts are long and visible, commercial at only 60 percent because AIP adoption is genuinely hard to forecast, and valuation confidence at 65 percent since everything runs through a price-to-sales multiple. Base case at 60 percent assumes government revenue growing a steady 18 to 20 percent while commercial accelerates to 40 to 45 percent as bootcamp customers convert to full deployments, with adjusted operating margin flat at 22 to 24 percent because sales and marketing spend eats the scale benefits. At 19x forward sales that supports $28, and importantly it assumes the stock trades on execution rather than hype, with the valuation debate capping multiple expansion. Bull at 25 percent needs a genuine inflection, three or four quarters of commercial growth above 60 percent or a major cloud or consulting partnership, which reframes the story from consulting-with-software to AI platform leader and pulls in a new institutional buyer base at 28x for $45. Given that asymmetry I land on hold with a bullish tilt rather than outright buy: add on a volume-confirmed break above $27.50 or a dip to the 50-day near $22.50, and treat a sustained loss of the 200-day around $20.00 as a hard stop. My honest critiques are that a P/S framework is fragile if the market regime rotates to value, that even the bear case 12x could prove too generous, and that PLTR's popularity invites confirmation bias in that subjective 25 percent bull weight. Leading indicators: total contract value growth, million-dollar customer counts, sales cycle length.

LVMH is a quality compounder priced against a macro variable I cannot see clearly, which is Chinese consumer behavior, so I set fundamental confidence at 85 percent but macro scenario confidence at only 60 percent, giving 70 percent overall. I model it with a 10,000-iteration Monte Carlo across Chinese GDP, EUR/USD, and high-net-worth spending growth. Base case at 60 percent assumes Chinese luxury spending up 4.5 percent, translating to roughly 6 percent growth in Fashion and Leather Goods, EUR/USD averaging 1.08 for about a 2 percent reported revenue headwind, and operating margin steady near 26.5 percent as price increases absorb inflation. At 25x forward earnings, the five-year average, that gives 850 euros, with the stock consolidating above the 200-day at 780 and a volume support node near 760. Bull at 25 percent needs a real Chinese fiscal package driving 12 to 15 percent luxury spending growth and EUR/USD down to 1.02 for a 3 to 4 percent tailwind, supporting 29x and 1,020 euros. Bear at 15 percent has HNWI spending down 10 percent, margins under 24 percent, and EUR/USD at 1.15 erasing 6 to 7 percent of reported growth, taking the stock to 640. Weighted that is 864.50 euros, so I initiate, entering 780 to 800, adding above 880 on volume, stopping on a weekly close below 720. The alternative reading I cannot dismiss is that this consolidation is distribution and the 24x multiple is the vulnerability rather than the quality signal. If 720 breaks, check Macau gaming revenue as an Asia proxy, the VIX above 25, and any Richemont or Kering pre-announcement.

Eli Lilly is a valuation-versus-execution problem where the execution is currently pristine, so I have to be careful not to let the chart do my thinking. The stock is above its 50-day EMA at $810, RSI at 68 is elevated but short of extreme, ADX above 40 confirms a genuinely strong trend, and OBV is accumulating. Base case at 60 percent assumes Mounjaro and Zepbound take major GLP-1 share with revenue from that franchise reaching $55 billion by 2029, company revenue compounding at 22 percent, operating margins widening 300 basis points to 38 percent, and donanemab approved but taken up cautiously given ARIA-E safety concerns. Applying a forward P/E of 45x, down from current levels as growth normalizes, gives $1050 over eighteen months. Bull at 25 percent takes GLP-1 to $75 billion, a 28 percent CAGR, and a sustained 55x for $1350, needing capacity ahead of schedule, unrestricted Zepbound coverage from big insurers, and clean orforglipron Phase 3 data. Bear at 15 percent has GLP-1 peaking at $35 billion, margins at 28 percent, and the premium collapsing to 30x for $680. Weighted, that is roughly $1036.25 and the 85 percent combined base-plus-bull probability justifies initiating, scaling in $840 to $860. But the valuation is the risk, and my DCF is sensitive enough that 100 basis points on the discount rate costs about $80 of base target, so a collar or long-dated calls make sense. Stop on a weekly close below the 200-day EMA near $650. Warning signs: total GLP-1 script growth slowing industry-wide, FDA adverse event spikes, PBM formulary exclusions.

Over a three to six month window Palantir's two segments deserve very different confidence weights, and stating that up front disciplines the rest. Government stability I would score at 85 percent because those contracts are sticky; the commercial growth thesis only 65 percent because sales cycles are long and execution uneven; fundamental health at 70 percent given lumpy revenue; overall about 68 percent. Base case at 60 percent has commercial revenue growing 35 to 40 percent and government 15 to 18 percent, GAAP profitability holding as stock-based compensation is controlled, forward P/E compressing into the 55 to 60x range on earnings growth, and ROE at 8 to 10 percent. The tape matches a stalemate: consolidation between the 200-day at $20 and prior highs at $27, MACD flat around zero, RSI mostly 40 to 60. At roughly 20x forward sales that supports $24.50, a modest premium to SaaS peers I can defend on market position. Bull at 25 percent needs commercial revenue past 50 percent and a landmark non-tech enterprise deal, with a 3x volume break above $27 taking it to $35 at 28x sales. Bear at 15 percent breaks $20 with negative OBV and resets to about 13x sales for $16. Since the current price effectively embeds the base case, the honest call is hold and accumulate on weakness, buying $20 to $22, trimming $26 to $27, stopping on a weekly close below $19.50. The lumpiness of large contracts is the analytical weak point. Failure signals: decelerating new commercial customer counts, gross margins slipping below 80 percent, and stock-based compensation creeping back up as a share of revenue.

Salesforce is now a maturity story dressed in growth-stock clothing, and the analysis has to price that honestly. Technically it is above the 200-day near $255 but consolidating after a pullback from highs; MACD is below signal though the histogram is bottoming, RSI at 48 is neutral with room to run, price sits at the middle Bollinger band, and there is real volume support at $250 to $260 coinciding with the 200-day. Base case at 55 percent assumes 9 to 11 percent revenue growth, 150 basis points of margin improvement from operational discipline, and Slack integrating adequately; at 23.5x forward non-GAAP earnings, its three-year average, that gives $270. Bull at 30 percent needs Einstein 1 adoption plus a broad enterprise software spending recovery and 300 basis points of margin expansion, worth 28x and $320. Bear at 15 percent is IT budget compression plus Dynamics 365 share gains at 19x for $215. Weighted that is $273.50, which lands almost exactly on today's price, so hold with a bullish tilt and add only on pullbacks toward the 200-day. Two things keep me from more conviction. First, everything hinges on management delivering the margin targets, and my confidence in forecasting macro IT spend is genuinely only about 50 percent. Second, I assign 65 percent odds to the alternative reading that decelerating revenue reflects saturation in core Sales Cloud rather than mere macro, in which case AI cannot fill the hole. My stress test - 30 percent operating margin instead of 32.5 percent with 7 percent growth - yields roughly $225. Watch RPO growth under 8 percent.

Zscaler near $180 is a good business at a price that leaves no room for error, which is why I put fundamental confidence at only 60 percent even though the growth is real. Base case at 60 percent has revenue moderating to a still-strong 30 to 35 percent, non-GAAP operating margin flat near 18 percent because Palo Alto and Microsoft pressure pricing, FCF margin around 20 percent, and the multiple settling at 12x to 14x forward sales. The chart agrees with a stalemate: a $160 to $200 range, the 50-day EMA acting as resistance while the 200-day near $165 holds as support, RSI pinned at the midpoint, Bollinger Bands contracting, and OBV flat with neither accumulation nor distribution. At 13.5x forward sales on FY2025 estimates that is $195. Bull at 25 percent essentially requires the Fed, roughly 75 basis points of cuts inside six months to lift long-duration assets, plus two quarters of billings growth above 40 percent, confirmed by a volume break above $205. Bear takes it to $130 at 9x sales on a break of $160 and a death cross. So I take a partial position here, add above $205 or on a successful retest of $165, and stop on a weekly close below $158. My self-critique is that the valuation offers no margin of safety and I may be favoring the best-of-breed technology story while underweighting how effectively larger vendors bundle security. The flat OBV could also be hiding institutional distribution in off-exchange blocks. Watch calculated billings first, then the mix of deals above $1 million ARR, then PANW and CRWD commentary on SASE.

Lululemon is the one name here where I end up with a fatter bear tail than bull, and I should let the numbers say why. Base case at 60 percent has North American same-store sales growing only 1 to 3 percent, international at 25 to 30 percent, gross margin defended at 57.5 percent by refusing broad promotions, and the multiple compressing to roughly 25x forward earnings for a $330 target, with the stock basing near $290 where the 2022 lows sit. The bull case only gets 15 percent because it requires North American comps above 5 percent, international above 40 percent on a real China rebound, and margins above 59 percent, which is a lot of things going right at once for $410. The bear gets 25 percent, more than double my usual weight, because Alo and Vuori are physically expanding, trade-down is plausible, and promotions taking gross margin under 56 percent would reset the stock toward $250 to $265 at about 20x. Weighted, that is $335, essentially where it trades, so Neutral/Hold. My confidence splits reveal the problem: 75 percent on fundamentals, only 60 percent on technicals given the downtrend, and 50 percent on the consumer, which is the swing factor. The interpretation I keep testing is whether elevated inventory signals a cyclical slowdown or a structural shift in aesthetic preference; I would put that at 60/40 toward slowdown. I also risk confirmation bias since the market already prices deceleration. North American comps are the single decisive metric: below zero validates the bear, above 5 percent flips me bullish.

Ahead of NVIDIA's Q3 print the asymmetry is not about whether the quarter is good but about whether a good quarter is enough given the multiple. Base case at 60 percent is a 5 to 10 percent revenue beat, EPS up 10 to 15 percent, and guidance in line to 5 percent above consensus. Technically the setup reads as a bullish flag above the 50-day EMA with weekly MACD above signal and OBV accumulating; a move to the upper Bollinger band near $580 fits. On forward earnings of $18 to $20 a share at 30 to 35x, versus the roughly 35x forward P/E today, I get $620. Bull at 25 percent requires a beat above 20 percent and a guidance raise above 15 percent, pulling FY2025 EPS estimates toward $25 to $28 and the stock to $750. Bear at 15 percent is a miss or guidance implying a plateau, with $410 as the target. The real risk I keep coming back to is a sell-the-news reaction on good numbers, because the price already embeds a lot. That drives the recommendation: those without a position should wait for the report rather than guess, holders should trim 10 to 15 percent to de-risk, and a call spread is the cleanest way to keep upside with defined cost. The alternative reading of the consolidation is distribution rather than a flag, and heavy volume on down days inside the range would support it. Failure triggers: a post-earnings close below the 50-day near $480, management using the words demand normalization, gross margin guidance under 75 percent, or a close below the pre-earnings low near $475.

A twelve-month Palantir view lets me build the scenarios off revenue estimates directly rather than pure narrative, so I run a 10,000-iteration simulation over commercial customer acquisition, average contract value, and government renewal rates. Base case at 60 percent has commercial revenue growing 35 to 40 percent with roughly 30 percent of AIP boot camps converting to paying customers, government growing 15 to 18 percent through renewals despite budget resolution risk, and operating margins widening 200 to 300 basis points on scale. On $3.1 billion of forward revenue at an 18x forward P/S multiple, in line with high-growth SaaS peers, I get $28, with the 200-day near $20 acting as a floor and RSI holding 50 to 60. Bear at 15 percent cuts forward revenue to $2.9 billion and compresses to 12x for $16, triggered by commercial customer growth falling under 20 percent, a restrictive continuing resolution, and persistent GAAP losses from stock-based compensation. Overall thesis confidence is only 65 percent because the AIP adoption curve is unknowable and hyperscalers could blunt it. The specific alternative I want on the record, at 25 percent probability, is that the surge in short-term commercial contracts represents trial usage rather than sticky platform adoption, which would look like growth right up until renewals fail. So a starter position at $23 to $25, add aggressively only above $27.50, and re-evaluate on a weekly close under $20. Warning signs: US commercial net adds below 30 for two quarters, average revenue per top-20 customer declining, and billings lagging revenue.

Lululemon around $305 poses the same question as before but with different weights, and here I land on a more constructive base than the sharper bear framing. Base case at 60 percent has North American growth in the low single digits offset by international at 35 to 40 percent, inventory managed well enough to hold gross margin near 58 percent, FY2024 revenue up 11 to 12 percent and EPS around $14.20, implying about 22x forward earnings at my $315 target against a five-year average of 25 to 30x adjusted for slower growth. The tape supports a range: the 200-day near $350 acting as resistance, support around $290, daily RSI stuck between 40 and 60, and the MACD histogram flat at zero. Bull at 25 percent needs North America re-accelerating to mid single digits, international above 50 percent, and gross margin above 59 percent, confirmed by a high-volume break of $350. I set macro confidence at only 50 percent, fundamentals at 75 percent, technicals at 70 percent, and overall thesis at 65 percent, which is honest about where the uncertainty sits. My self-criticism is leaning on the brand narrative; premium consumers are not recession-proof and loyalty erodes quickly when the aesthetic shifts, so 15 percent on the bear may be light. The inventory build is the crux - management calls it strategic, but a bullwhip reading is plausible. Stance is neutral and hold, buying only on a dip to $290 to $295, with a weekly close below $288 as the stop. Check Similarweb traffic, card spending data, and whether management's tone shifts to managing headwinds.

EEM is not a stock-picking problem, it is a dollar and China problem, and the technicals are already telling me which way the wind blows: price below the 200-day, weekly RSI under 50, and a multi-month descending channel with support near $38.50. Base case at 60 percent has the Fed staying higher for longer, the dollar staying firm, and Chinese stimulus putting in a floor without igniting growth, with index EPS growth of only 2 to 4 percent. The aggregate P/E of about 12x looks cheap against the S&P at roughly 21x, but that discount is compensation for lower growth and higher risk, not a free lunch, so my target is $37.50, about 5 percent lower, at 75 percent confidence. The bull at only 15 percent needs both a trillion-dollar-plus Chinese fiscal package and core PCE under 2.5 percent for two months to weaken the dollar; multiple expansion to 14x plus 5 to 7 percent of currency translation gets $46.00. I give the bear 25 percent, more than the bull, because a Taiwan escalation or deepening property crisis is a live risk, and history says a 10 percent DXY surge maps to EEM underperforming the S&P by 12 to 15 percent over the next six months. That skew means no long here. Short below $38.50 targeting $37.50 then $33.00, stop at $40.00, and only go long on a volume break above the 200-day near $41.50. My blind spot is treating EEM as monolithic when India or Brazil strength could offset China. If stopped out, check copper-gold, EM bond fund flows, and the KOSPI and TAIEX.

This Salesforce view runs on a slightly different price base than my other pass at the name, but the structure of the argument is the same: an entrenched, non-discretionary platform whose upside now depends on AI monetization I cannot yet measure. Base case at 60 percent assumes Einstein Copilot and Data Cloud adding an estimated 150 to 200 basis points to revenue growth by the second half of 2024, revenue up 10 to 11 percent, operating margin expanding 200 basis points to about 32.5 percent, ROE improving to 14 percent, with GDP at 1.5 to 2.0 percent and fed funds near 4.75 percent producing cautious 3 to 5 percent IT budget growth. At 25x forward non-GAAP earnings, slightly under the five-year average, that gives $285, with the stock consolidating $250 to $290 above the 200-day, RSI at 45 to 60. Bull at 25 percent needs a 20 percent Copilot attach rate within nine months rather than the 12 to 18 months I assume, adding 300 to 400 basis points of growth and re-rating to 30x for $340. The vulnerability I have to state plainly is that there is essentially no historical precedent for monetizing generative AI in CRM, so my 150 to 200 basis point estimate is an educated guess. I also assign 35 percent to the reading that this consolidation is distribution rather than accumulation, supported by flat OBV. The reassuring part is the stress test: even a 15 percent drop in new bookings holds valuation above $230 because more than 80 percent of revenue is recurring. Watch billings versus revenue, RPO, and Microsoft's commentary.

Lockheed is the opposite of the AI names in this set: the question is not how fast it grows but how reliably it converts backlog, so my confidence sits at 75 percent, high on fundamentals and only medium on near-term price. Technically it is caught between signals, above the 200-day near $445 but below the 50-day near $465, consolidating $450 to $475 with RSI at 48, a slightly negative MACD histogram, and contracting Bollinger Bands that suggest a move is coming without saying which way. The volume shelf at $450 to $455 is what makes support credible. Fundamentally there is a lot to like: P/E around 17.5x in line with its own five-year average, ROE near 55 percent, ROCE about 18 percent, FCF yield of 5.5 percent covering a 2.6 percent dividend plus buybacks, debt to equity manageable at 1.5, and a record backlog above $160 billion giving three to five years of revenue visibility. Growth is low single digits and that is fine; predictability is the product. The bear case at 15.0x forward earnings gives $410, and the transmission is concrete - a 5 percent cut to DoD procurement takes 2 to 3 percent off forward revenue, and each 100 basis points of long-term growth expectation moves my DCF by about $15 a share. So accumulate on weakness, ideally $450 to $455, base target $495 over 12 to 18 months, stop on a weekly close below $440. The honest vulnerability is that this thesis needs elevated geopolitical tension to persist. Watch book-to-bill under 1.0, margins under 15 percent, and NDAA line items on F-35, PAC-3, and GMLRS.
